entities.name: Baitul Futuh Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Baitul Futuh Mosque (House of Victories) in Morden, London, United Kingdom, inaugurated in 2003 — the largest mosque in Western Europe at time of completion, designed by the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community's in-house architects and built primarily by volunteer labor from the Ahmadiyya community worldwide — is one of the most significant Islamic monuments in the United Kingdom and a symbol of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community's Western presence and its distinct theological tradition.

The Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, founded in British India in 1889 by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (who claimed to be the Mahdi and promised Messiah), is a heterodox Islamic movement considered apostate by mainstream Sunni and Shia Islam but claims approximately 10-20 million followers worldwide. The community has been persecuted in Pakistan (where Ahmadis are legally barred from calling themselves Muslims), Indonesia, and other Muslim-majority countries, making the UK — where they have been free to practice since establishing a presence in the early 20th century — their most important Western base.

Baitul Futuh's construction, with its dome, minarets, and capacity for 10,000 worshippers, represents the Ahmadiyya community's most prominent architectural statement in the West. The mosque complex includes a library, museum, offices, and residential quarters, making it a comprehensive Islamic community center. Its inauguration was attended by 30,000 people from 100 countries, demonstrating the global reach of the Ahmadiyya network centered on their London caliph.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Baitul Futuh Mosque — Western Europe's largest mosque at completion, headquarters of the Ahmadiyya caliphate in London, built by volunteer community labor, and a symbol of Ahmadiyya religious freedom in the West contrasting with persecution in Muslim-majority states — is the most important Ahmadiyya monument in the Western world.
